scope: One existing owner receives missing fictional sample/comparison/decision context within its existing report-card note. All earlier note text/order and links are retained. One earlier NCI access assertion is corrected in provenance, with actual reading depth. No new empirical result, id, link, relation, summary, TLDR or registration.

before: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

Figure reading (fictional): the same DNA call, a T in the sequence A C T G A, is copied into Report A, Report B and Report C, which is one observation reported three times. A separate RNA assay showing a splice junction is a new measurement that answers a new question, and it does not by itself confirm the DNA call.

Figure reading (fictional Target Q): specimen S at time T1 supplies bulk RNA, where Q is abundant, and a tissue image, where Q protein is seen in normal vessel cells. Whether malignant cells carry accessible Q is unresolved, a model-imputed Q is labelled as an estimate rather than a measurement, and a different specimen or time point is not paired evidence.

Genome, transcriptome and proteome name DNA, RNA and protein collections. An omics profile measures many features within a layer, subject to its coverage and capture limits; it does not necessarily inspect every molecule. Molecular layer and spatial or cellular resolution answer different questions. Multi-omic integration relates the measured layers, with their specimen and analysis context retained, rather than turning a larger number of assays into a universal measure of certainty.

Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

A practical report reading starts with six questions: what specimen, region, date and treatment context were sampled; what object and units were measured with which assay version; whether the result is signed clinical, preliminary, research or model-predicted evidence; which controls or reference support the comparison; what remains unmeasured; and which actual decision could change. A missing field is a question to resolve, not a fact to assume. For fictional pretreatment bulk RNA, high R relative to a stated reference supports captured expression in that mixture. Calling it a surface target remains an interpretation until the contributing cells and accessible protein are established; selectivity, dependence and treatment benefit need their own evidence. Molecular layer and resolution are separate axes. Mapping 500 RNA targets in one section adds location relative to a pooled RNA result, while the measured layer remains RNA. It does not add a membrane-protein or functional measurement.

An entirely fictional core-biopsy report lists invasive carcinoma of no special type, grade 3; ER and PR below 1 percent; HER2 IHC one-plus; Ki-67 positivity of 60 percent; stromal TILs of 30 percent; PD-L1 22C3 combined positive score 15; and a supported TP53 missense finding at VAF 38 percent on a tumour-only panel. These observations retain separate rules and denominators. The diagnosis describes the sampled region; the receptor results support a triple-negative category and low HER2 staining under the stated testing rules, without establishing a particular drug benefit. Ki-67 positivity is not a treatment-selection rule here. The stromal score is an eligible-area assessment, not proof of recognition, and CPS is its own defined stain score rather than a universal immune percentage. VAF is not inherited status, cancer-cell fraction or measured variant function. KEYNOTE-355 tested pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in previously untreated advanced TNBC; its CPS-at-least-ten group had median PFS 9.7 versus 5.6 months, hazard ratio 0.65. KEYNOTE-522 enrolled high-risk early TNBC regardless of PD-L1 status. A score cannot transfer benefit between those settings. None of these invented values is a patient observation or a prescription.

before.editedBy: OnCo systematic education audit, round 3 (spatial and computational content): Crossref and Europe PMC identity checks, abstracts and selected full texts read
before.note: Argelaguet 2018 (PMID 29925568), Risso 2014 (PMID 25150836) and Mertins 2016 (PMID 27251275): DOI and PMID resolved and matched on title, authors and year; the 200-sample leukaemia application, the biological-and-technical factor description, the depth-only normalisation finding and the 105/77 breast cancer counts were read in the abstracts. The paired-versus-unpaired, imputation-label and patient-level-split points are the lesson's methodological principles, not findings of those papers. The lesson's NCI biomarker-testing citation was not adopted: the page text does not state that a molecular match fails to ensure benefit.

after.editedBy: OnCo systematic education audit, round 3 (spatial and computational content): Crossref and Europe PMC identity checks, abstracts and selected full texts read
after.note: Argelaguet 2018 (PMID 29925568), Risso 2014 (PMID 25150836) and Mertins 2016 (PMID 27251275): DOI and PMID resolved and matched on title, authors and year; the 200-sample leukaemia application, the biological-and-technical factor description, the depth-only normalisation finding and the 105/77 breast cancer counts were read in the abstracts. The paired-versus-unpaired, imputation-label and patient-level-split points are the lesson's methodological principles, not findings of those papers. The NCI biomarker-testing page was re-read in selected complete paragraphs on 13 November 2026: its matching-treatment discussion says that a matching biomarker does not ensure benefit. This supports the qualified evidence boundary here; no complete current test inventory or whole-page clinical verification is claimed. The report-card example is fictional.
